title: The Tea That Costs You Something

blocks.p: The tea was genmaicha, toasted and ordinary, and it was the most dangerous thing Rei had drunk all week precisely because it was so ordinary. Kishin understood that the way to a guarded person is not through fear. It is through the small kindness they have been too busy to receive. Rinka poured and asked, in the host's voice, whether he had eaten. Whether he was sleeping. Whether the heat was keeping him up. Each question landed in the part of him that no one had asked since the fourteenth, the part that had been holding his brother's vanishing alone in a city of nine million. He had to set the cup down to keep his hand from being read.

This was what it wanted, and it was never money. It wanted him to be comfortable in its presence. Comfort was how the erosion got in, one warm hour at a time, until the day a person found they could not think a hard thought about Kanna-sensei without a small grief at the disloyalty of it.
Rei made himself ask the only question worth the climb. Who drew the battery down?

Rinka answered without coyness, because Kishin gained nothing by withholding and everything by being the one who told him. "Both," she said. "The Healer comes for it gently, in the small hours. What he takes, he uses to soften the seams in Kita so they will part without tearing. A surgeon thinning a wall into a membrane he can lift clean. And the boy who preaches draws for me, in great greedy pulls, because I do not want the wall lifted. I want it broken. The held breath let out all at once." She poured more tea he had not asked for. "The Healer thinks he steals from me. I let him. A thief who drinks from my cup is a thief I can always find." She let the next part land softly. "And lately the grief has been coming faster. Two of us pulling at the same harvest is very good for the harvest."
"He's hunting you," Rei said. It was a guess, and it was right.

"He means to kill me." She said it the way people mention rain. "A demon can only be killed on this side from inside a body. That is what your brother is to him, you understand. A hand to do it with." The kind eyes rested on him. "It is a door I have not yet had to close. There is time."
Rei read the room while she spoke, and the thing in her did not seem to mind being read. He did not think it was afraid. He thought, quietly, that it should be.

And there it was, the thing he had come up the stairs not knowing he needed. His brother's captor and the cult's god were not two unrelated horrors. They were two ends of one rope, and the rope was being paid out from this room. He should have felt the click of a case closing. Instead he felt the cup warm in his hands and Rinka's patient eyes on him and the terrible domestic peace of the moment. He had already begun to owe her. Not for a service rendered, but for a comfort accepted. The bill for comfort is the hardest of all to read, because it never arrives as a number. It arrives as a softness he did not used to have, in the exact place where he used to keep his edge.

Around them the circle was ending. People were stretching their legs and murmuring. An older woman in an apron moved round the ring with a lacquer box, and each person laid an envelope in it with a name written on the front. She carried the box to a cupboard and locked it and put the key on a cord round her neck. Then she checked the clock against a handwritten timetable taped inside the cupboard door and wrote something on it.

blocks.cap: The circle's Keeper, who holds the money, the room and the schedule

blocks.p: "Our Keeper," Rinka said, following his eyes. "She keeps the house. The money, the room, the schedule, the photographs on the wall. Without her none of this would stand up for a week."

Gin had a line for that too. A cult can survive losing its Voice. It rarely survives losing its Keeper, because the Keeper holds the cultivation itself. Rei looked at the woman in the apron, at her tired careful hands, and understood that she believed she was doing the most loving thing she had ever done.

He let his reading go outward through the building. The ring kneeling here tonight were the Faithful. They knew there was a presence. They served it and brought the offerings, and they had walked far enough to be locked. Below them, spread across the ward, were the ones who never climbed the humming stairs at all. The weekly letting-go circles in borrowed municipal rooms, the grief meetings with free tea and paper tissues. Gin called that outer ring the Unknowing. They were the cover, the numbers and the recruiting surface, and the thing at the centre took a thin low feeding from every one of those rooms without anyone noticing.
"And your Voice?" Rei asked. "Who does it speak through, out there?"

"Our Voice is in the city tonight," Rinka said. "In a drained pool, with forty people who love him." She meant Kaito. Gin had written that the Voice is often a genuine medium and the most thoroughly deceived person in the room. Rei thought of the courier preaching in the dead hour and was not sure Kaito was deceived any longer. He thought Kaito might simply be empty.
"And the one who saw it first? The one it all started with?"

Rinka touched her own chest, lightly, over the river stone. "The first to see the far shore," she said. "She is with us still. In spirit." Gin had a word for that one as well. The Touched, whose original experience the whole doctrine is built around. Sometimes the Touched and the Voice are the same person. Sometimes the Touched is dead and the cult is built on the memory of what happened to her. Rei looked at the stone and did not reach for it again.

The rites were laid out in front of him if he chose to see them. The naming, when the ring first called the presence the Far Shore and spoke of it as a being owed devotion. The offering, the envelopes in the lacquer box, the names of the dead given every week. The proof, the cold shimmer at the centre, the moment each mourner heard a beloved voice in the ear exactly when doubt would have come. And somewhere past those, kept private, the binding rite. Gin said that if you could find a group's binding rite, you had found the exact line between its victims and its participants.

Rei named a price, because he would not leave owing a thing he could not see. He had watched what unseen debts did to the people in his brother's ledger. Kishin smiled through Rinka's mouth and told him the cost in the only currency it kept.

It did not want his blood or his service or his soul. Those were merchants' words for merchants' appetites. It wanted the next grief he carried to come here first. Not all his grief. Just the next fresh one, whenever it landed, before he had decided alone what to do with it. The way the man from Sumida had brought his. The way the widow had brought hers. Bring it warm to the circle, kneel in the eastern seat, and let the room take its weight off him for one evening, and the intelligence he had bought tonight would be paid in full. It was, she pointed out gently, the same agreement everyone in the ring had made. And look how lightly they carried their losses now.
So that was the binding rite. Not a blade or an oath. A seat on the eastern side and one evening's relief.

blocks.cap: A circle of chairs, the funnel that draws people down

blocks.p: Rei mapped it then, the way he would map a poisoning, on the widow who had whispered to him. Gin had walked the funnel backward with enough former members to draw it, and it was the same shape almost every time. First the hook. A real experience of the veil. Her husband's voice in the tide at the seawall, a thing that had actually happened to her, and you cannot argue someone out of a thing that actually happened to them. Then the meeting. Someone who did not say she had imagined it. Someone who took both her hands and said I know what that was, and you are not alone, and there are others. The validation is the recruitment, Gin had written. Everything after is detail. Then the frame. A name for it, a doctrine, the far shore where the dead wait, and a being at the centre who could reach them and was owed something for it. Then the deepening. Come once. Come weekly. Bring a name in an envelope. Stop seeing the sister who said this was not healthy. A flat demand would be refused. A slope is walked. And last the lock. The thing you cannot take back. The eastern seat.
No one joins, Gin had written under his drawing of it. People are drawn down.

And then, because he was honest, Rei ran the same funnel on himself. The hook was the kitchen at 3:47 and a brother gone. The meeting was tonight, a voice asking if he had eaten. The frame was being told he was expected, that his name was already in her book. The deepening was a second cup of tea. The lock was the price on the table.

He thought of Gin. He thought of the exact grief he was carrying up these stairs and down them, the one with his brother's name on it, still unspent, still his. It was the only thing keeping him walking toward Gin while the whole city walked away. What Kishin had asked for, in its perfect hospitality, was the one grief that must never be soothed. The day Rei stopped hurting over Gin was the day he stopped coming for him. The demon knew this. That was the elegance of the price. It had not asked him to betray his brother. It had asked him to be comforted about him. It trusted that he was tired enough, after a week of this heat and this dread and this aloneness, to want comfort more than he wanted the edge that comfort cost.
"You keep your word, I suppose," Rei said.

"Always." Rinka tilted her head. "I am not like your brother's thief, who signs forms for the privilege of being trusted. Or the little contracted one in Kōenji, who keeps his Usami like a houseplant and waters him every morning." The smile did not change. "I did not keep Fukai like that. There was no need."

Rei had read that name on a train only days ago, in pencil, down the margin of a CVD card. Ren kept what was left of Usami. Kishin had kept nothing of Rinka at all. It had put the lights out one by one, and it wanted him to know it had felt nothing while it did.

Rinka set the iron pot down with a soft iron sound. Around them the congregation was gathering their sandals and saying their goodnights, ordinary people stepping out into the Obon dark a little lighter than they came. Not one of them looked back at the centre that had carried them. Rei could leave the same way. He could take everything he had learned tonight and owe nothing but the next ache. The next ache was months away, surely. Surely he would be stronger by then. That was exactly the size of the lie the room was built to make feel like sense.

He stood up. He did not say yes. He did not say no, either, because he did not trust his voice to stay his own. The tea had gone cold in his hands and he had not noticed it cooling, which was, he thought, the whole demonstration.
He was at the door, one hand on the frame, when she spoke again. She did not raise her voice. She never needed to.
"Saturday, Rei-kun," Kanna-sensei said. "Bring whatever you are carrying by then. The eastern seat will be warm."
He went down the humming stairs past the child's sandals, and he did not let himself count how many days it was until Saturday.
